verdict.reasoning:
The claim's two factual observations are accurate, but they describe leading whitespace only, not content, and the instruction is to reject differences that are page-break furniture or formatting.

WHAT I INDEPENDENTLY CONFIRMED.
PDF (spec_p78.png, 300 dpi, printed folio 48). The lettered markers b), c), d), e) all sit at the same left position, one indent step in from the running head 'ISO/IEC 1989:2023 (E)'. The markers 1. 2. 3. 4. 5. 6. sit one further step in, beneath 'c) The following rules apply for the purpose of matching:'. Under item 4 the sub-markers are printed 'a.' and 'b.' (letter + period), one step deeper again. The page opens with the runover of item a) ('operand that precedes the reserved word BY is compared to an equivalent number of contiguous library text-words.') and closes mid-sentence inside e) ('The next successive library text-word'). So the PDF layout is as the claim states.
Markdown (specs/ISO_COBOL.md). Measured leading whitespace: line 3469 '   a) The leftmost library text-word ...' = 3 spaces; b), c), d), e) = 0; items 1. through 6. = 0; the sub-items under 4 ('   a. The two representations ...', '   b. In the content of the literal ...') = 3; the NOTE = 3. So the markdown is also as the claim states.

WHY THIS IS NOT A CONTENT DISCREPANCY.
1. Not one character of normative text differs. I compared the rendered page against the transcription end to end: the runover of a), all of b), c), items 1.-6., the a./b. sub-items under 4, the NOTE, d) and e) are all present, complete, and word-for-word. Nothing is missing, added, reordered, or reworded. The only textual deviation anywhere is the NOTE's wide printed gap ('NOTE    Because') collapsed to one space, which is itself whitespace.
2. Every structural label survives verbatim. The markers are the hierarchy in an ISO text -- 7.2.3.4 GR 9 c) 3) is cited by those very labels, not by indentation. The transcription preserves 9), a), b), c), d), e), f), g), 1. through 6., and a./b., in the printed order and in the printed marker style (paren for the a)-g) and 9)-13) levels, period for the 1.-6. and a./b. levels). A reader or a citation tool recovers the identical parent/child relation from the labels alone. Meaning is unchanged.
3. This is page-slicing furniture, not a page-78 corruption. The flattening is the transcription's global behaviour at page boundaries, and mis-scoping it to page 78 would be wrong. Document-wide there are 572 column-0 lettered items against 777 indented ones. In this very list the flattening continues onto page 79 for f) and g), and the PARENT-level rules 10), 11), 12), 13) are likewise at column 0 -- the same depth as their own children b)-e). The genuine outlier is a), which is indented only because it happened to land on the same OCR page as its parent 9). There is no page-78-specific defect here; there is one uniform convention with one boundary-local artifact.

WHERE THE CLAIM OVERREACHES.
The 'why it matters' asserts the parent/child relation 'is lost'. It is not lost -- it is carried by the labels, which is where ISO puts it. The rationale describes a rendering-depth difference in a viewer, and a viewer's indentation is precisely the formatting layer this reconciliation is instructed to disregard. Under the stated bar -- reject when the difference is formatting or page-break furniture, and when meaning is unchanged -- this does not qualify.

One caveat recorded honestly, since it is the strongest form of the claim: at column 0 the markers 1. through 6. do render as their own ordered list, and elsewhere in the same clause the syntax rules of 7.2.3.3 also use column-0 '1.' through '13.'. A purely mechanical consumer that keyed off indentation rather than off the labels could in principle confuse the two levels. That is a cosmetic/tooling consideration for a possible document-wide indentation normalization pass, not evidence that page 78's content diverges from the PDF. It does not.
verdict.corrected_description: Not a content discrepancy. The claim's observations about both sources are factually correct -- the PDF prints b)-e) one indent level under general rule 9) and 1.-6. one level deeper under c), while the markdown places b), c), d), e) and 1. through 6. at column 0 with only page 77's a) indented 3 spaces -- but the difference is leading whitespace alone. Every word of normative text and every structural label (9), a)-g), 1.-6., a./b., NOTE) is present, correct, in order, and in the printed marker style, so the parent/child relation is fully recoverable from the labels, which is how ISO cites these rules. The flattening is the transcription's document-wide page-sliced-OCR convention rather than a page-78 defect: 572 lettered items sit at column 0 across the file, the same flattening carries onto page 79 for f) and g), and even the parent rules 10)-13) are at column 0; the real outlier is a), indented only because it shared an OCR page with its parent 9). At most this supports a document-wide indentation-normalization cleanup, filed against the transcription convention as a whole and not as a page-78 misplaced-content finding.
